cf.title: pg_rewind: Remove recovery at the start of rewind

input.subject: pg_rewind: Remove recovery at the start of rewind

verdict_reasoning: The goal is reasonable and comes with a measurement, but the proposal removes a safety step without saying what replaces its side effects. replication-ondisk-2 is decisive: crash recovery used to bring pg_control up to date before pg_rewind read it, and message #1 names no replacement. maintenance-fit-1 and replication-ondisk-3 raise the same kind of gap for end-of-recovery actions and for the postmaster.pid interlock. All are answerable, and only one message is visible, so confidence is low.

brief.title: pg_rewind: skip crash recovery on an unclean target by scanning its WAL
brief.problem: When the target was not shut down cleanly, pg_rewind starts it in single-user mode and replays all WAL from the last checkpoint before rewinding. Much of that redo goes into relation files that pg_rewind then overwrites from the source or removes. This costs time for users who rewind a crashed or immediately stopped old primary.
brief.proposed_design: pg_rewind already reads target WAL from the last common checkpoint to build the page map, and the patch extends that scan to find the end of target WAL, so it no longer needs a shutdown checkpoint or minRecoveryPoint. It finds the checkpoint before the divergence point by following the record chain backwards, with a forward scan from the control-file checkpoint as fallback. The target must still be stopped, and pg_rewind checks for a running postmaster.
user_visible_surface: The --no-ensure-shutdown option of pg_rewind is removed.
pg_rewind accepts a target that was not shut down cleanly and no longer starts it in single-user mode.
pg_rewind rejects a target with a live postmaster and removes a stale postmaster.pid whose PID no longer exists.
author_claims: A local benchmark shows about 25% to 37% shorter run time for 100 MB to 2000 MB of uncheckpointed target data, about 1.5 times faster.
The saving comes from skipping redo into files that pg_rewind later restores or removes, since both versions read target WAL.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible, and nobody has replied. The CommitFest entry needs review, needed a rebase in September and has moved to a second CommitFest.
unclear: The patch prose does not say how pg_rewind finds a safe end of WAL when the last segment is torn or partly written.
The proposal does not say what replaces the control-file state, minRecoveryPoint and timeline fields that crash recovery used to update before rewind and recovery after it.
The patch prose does not say why removing --no-ensure-shutdown is acceptable for scripts that pass it, or whether it could stay as a no-op.
The proposal does not say how removing a stale postmaster.pid avoids a PID reused by another process or a postmaster in another container.
The patch prose does not say whether the documentation changes, since no doc files appear in the touched files.
The benchmark does not give the workload, storage or the share of time spent in redo versus copying.

prior_attempts.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL
prior_attempts.quote: But I do not think we can do that, because (1) those WAL records might do important things like update the control file and (2) the server will not be OK with ignoring those WAL records even if pg_rewind decides that they are not important.
prior_attempts.reason: Robert Haas said the premise is wrong: the shutdown checkpoint updates the control file, which matters when deciding whether servers are in sync, and the server itself refuses to follow the new timeline. A clean shutdown also writes a RUNNING_XACTS record, which the patch did not skip. A later version from another poster did not address these points, and the entry was withdrawn.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P8 skipped shutdown-only records when finding the end of target WAL. This proposal reads every record but no longer runs the recovery that updated the control file, so only the control-file part of the P8 objection carries over.

objections.title: Target timeline and control-file fields are read without recovery updating them
objections.failure_scenario: A node is promoted, writes on the new timeline, and crashes before its first checkpoint after promotion completes. Its pg_control still shows the old timeline in checkPointCopy. pg_rewind builds the target history from that stale timeline, picks the wrong divergence point or reports that no rewind is needed, and the node later follows the new primary with diverged blocks.
objections.argument: Crash recovery used to end with a shutdown checkpoint that brought pg_control's checkpoint, timeline and minRecoveryPoint up to date before pg_rewind read them. [P8] was withdrawn partly because WAL after divergence updates the control file, and pg_rewind's sync decision depends on that. The proposal does not say which control-file fields pg_rewind now trusts as-is and which it derives from the WAL scan.
objections.author_must_show: For a target that crashed after promotion but before a checkpoint, which timeline does pg_rewind use, and how is it derived?

precedents.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL

critic.reasoning: Today the checkpoint written when single-user recovery shuts down updates the timeline in pg_control before pg_rewind reads it, and the proposal names no replacement. P8 supports only the control-file point, because this patch reads those records and does not skip them.

objections.title: pg_rewind gets a second end-of-WAL rule that must match the server's
objections.failure_scenario: An old primary crashes with a torn last segment or an aborted contrecord. The pg_rewind scan stops at a different LSN than crash recovery would, so pg_rewind reports "no rewind required" or misses blocks. The server then refuses the new timeline or runs with stale pages, and the operator finds out only at startup or later.
objections.argument: Today the server decides where an unclean target's WAL ends, and pg_rewind reads the result from a shutdown checkpoint. The patch moves that decision into parsexlog.c, so any later change to end-of-WAL handling or to records with side effects must also be made in pg_rewind. A missed change does not fail loudly. [P8], from the same area and author, was withdrawn after a reviewer said pg_rewind's view of end of WAL cannot differ from the server's, and message #1 does not explain why that concern no longer applies.
objections.author_must_show: How does the patch make sure the pg_rewind end-of-WAL point always equals the point crash recovery would reach, and what test fails if the two drift apart?

precedents.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL

critic.reasoning: Record validation is shared xlogreader code and cannot drift, but the end-of-recovery actions live only in the server and the proposal names no test tying the two together. P8 concerned skipping records, which this patch does not do, so it is not support. An explanation or test can answer this.

objections.title: Stale postmaster.pid removal by PID check alone can expose a live cluster
objections.failure_scenario: The data directory is on a shared volume, and a postmaster runs on it in another container or PID namespace. pg_rewind sees no such PID, removes postmaster.pid and rewrites relation files under the running server. The data is corrupted, and nobody notices until that server crashes or returns wrong rows.
objections.argument: Under the old design, a single-user postgres start protected the directory with the server's lock-file logic, which also checks whether the old shared memory segment is still in use. The commit message says pg_rewind removes postmaster.pid "when its PID no longer exists", which is a weaker check. The proposal does not say how it handles PID reuse or postmasters in another namespace.
objections.author_must_show: What interlock beyond a PID existence check stops pg_rewind from removing postmaster.pid and writing to a data directory that a postmaster in another namespace still uses?

critic.reasoning: The server's lock-file check has the same gap for a separate PID namespace, so the container scenario is not new. The shared memory check does differ: a dead postmaster with live orphaned backends passes a PID-only check, and the proposal names no interlock.

objections.title: Removing --no-ensure-shutdown breaks existing failover scripts
objections.failure_scenario: A failover tool such as a cluster manager runs pg_rewind --no-ensure-shutdown after promoting a standby. After the upgrade, pg_rewind exits with an unknown-option error. The old primary is not rejoined, and the operator finds out during the next failover, when the cluster runs without a standby.
objections.argument: The commit message removes the option outright because pg_rewind no longer starts the target. Users who pass it asked for exactly what the new code does: skip the single-user start. Postgres usually keeps such options as accepted no-ops for some releases, or deprecates them first. The touched files include no documentation, so the reference page would still list the option and the clean-shutdown requirement.
objections.author_must_show: Why can --no-ensure-shutdown not stay as an accepted no-op, with the pg_rewind documentation updated to match the new behaviour?

critic.reasoning: The proposal gives no reason for removing the option instead of keeping it as a no-op, and the script failure is concrete. The claim that Postgres usually keeps such options is overstated, since major releases have removed client options before.

objections.title: No field evidence that crash recovery dominates real rewind time
objections.failure_scenario: An operator rewinds a crashed old primary during failover. The rewind may finish a few seconds sooner, but every rewind now relies on pg_rewind's own end-of-WAL scan instead of the server's recovery code. If that scan mishandles a case that server recovery handles, the operator finds out when the rewound node fails to start or diverges.
objections.argument: The only evidence is one local benchmark in message #1, and nobody has replied. It saves under 1.5 s for 100 MB and about 19 s for 2000 MB. Message #1 gives no workload, storage, or redo share, and cites no user report that this step slows failover. The commit message drops the dependency on a shutdown checkpoint and minRecoveryPoint, so the new path may also cover clean-shutdown targets, which gain nothing.
objections.author_must_show: Which production failovers spend a large share of pg_rewind time in single-user crash recovery, and how many seconds would this save there?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 offers one local benchmark without workload or storage details and cites no user report, so demand is not shown. The remark about clean-shutdown targets is speculation and should be dropped.

refuted.title: Skipping redo leaves the target control file stale, as in P8
refuted.failure_scenario: An old primary is promoted, writes its end-of-recovery record on a new timeline, and is stopped immediately before a checkpoint updates the control file. pg_rewind v1 reads the stale timeline and checkpoint from the control file. It then computes the wrong divergence point or reports that no rewind is needed, and the error shows only when the target fails to start as a standby.
refuted.argument: In P8, also on finding the end of target WAL, the recorded objection was that target WAL records may update the control file, and the server will not ignore them. Today, crash recovery in single-user mode brings the control file timeline, checkpoint and minRecoveryPoint up to date before pg_rewind reads them. Message #1 removes that step but says only that WAL scanning replaces the shutdown checkpoint and minRecoveryPoint. It does not say how pg_rewind derives the target timeline when the control file is behind its own WAL.
refuted.author_must_show: When the control file of an unclean target is behind its WAL, for example after a promotion with no checkpoint since, how does pg_rewind obtain the correct timeline and checkpoint?

precedents.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-2, which states the same promoted-then-crashed scenario and names the stale control-file field.

refuted.title: pg_rewind deleting postmaster.pid replaces the server's own lock check
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator runs pg_rewind from one container against a data directory that a postmaster in another container still uses. The postmaster's PID does not exist in pg_rewind's PID namespace, so pg_rewind removes postmaster.pid and rewrites files under a live server. The corruption appears only after the next restart or failover.
refuted.argument: Today the single-user postgres start goes through the server's own lock-file logic, which handles cases that a plain PID check does not. The patch replaces this with pg_rewind removing postmaster.pid when its PID is not found. Only the postmaster has ever managed that file, and the proposal does not say how PID reuse or PID namespaces are handled. Refusing to run and telling the user to remove the file would keep the old contract.
refuted.author_must_show: What makes the stale postmaster.pid check as safe as the server's own lock check, and why should pg_rewind remove the file instead of refusing to run?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-3, which also names the shared memory check that the single-user start performs today.

refuted.title: End of target WAL now comes from a frontend scan, not server recovery
refuted.failure_scenario: An old primary stops with an immediate stop, and its last WAL segment holds a torn record, a recycled segment tail or a missing continuation record. The new scan stops earlier than the flushed WAL, so blocks changed by later records are left out of the page map. Those blocks keep target-only contents, and the user finds the corruption only when queries return wrong data.
refuted.argument: Today the end of the page-map scan is a shutdown checkpoint or minRecoveryPoint. The server wrote both after running its own end-of-WAL logic, including the overwrite-contrecord handling. The patch removes that dependency and makes pg_rewind decide where flushed WAL ends, but the prose in message #1 and the commit message does not say how it handles a torn or partly written last segment. If the scan stops too early, blocks are silently missed, and nothing reports an error.
refuted.author_must_show: How does the scan decide where valid target WAL ends, and why can it never stop before WAL whose changes may already be in data files?

critic.reasoning: pg_rewind reads WAL with the same xlogreader validation that crash recovery uses, so both stop at the same first invalid record. Under the WAL-before-data rule, data files hold no changes from records beyond valid flushed WAL, so no block is missed.

refuted.title: Removing --no-ensure-shutdown breaks existing failover scripts
refuted.failure_scenario: A failover tool passes --no-ensure-shutdown to pg_rewind. After an upgrade to the new release, pg_rewind exits with an unknown-option error during an incident, and the old primary is not rewound until someone edits the script.
refuted.argument: The commit message removes the option outright. Message #1 does not mention a deprecation period or keeping it as a no-op. Client tools usually keep accepted options across releases for this reason, and dropping one saves very little code.
refuted.author_must_show: Why not keep --no-ensure-shutdown as an accepted no-op with a notice, so existing failover scripts keep working?

refuted.title: No committer who knows recovery has looked at this yet
refuted.failure_scenario: The patch is committed after only light review. A year later a user reports a corrupted rewind after an immediate stop, and the only people who could debug the interaction between the new scan and xlogreader were never part of the design.
refuted.argument: The thread has one message and no replies, and the entry has already moved to a second CommitFest. The change replaces a safety step, server crash recovery, with tool-side logic, so its owner needs to know both recovery and pg_rewind. The proposal does not show such a person engaged or the author staying on for follow-up fixes.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with recovery and xlogreader has agreed that pg_rewind should own end-of-WAL detection for unclean targets?

critic.reasoning: A thread with no replies yet describes any new patch and belongs in the committability field. The rubric says weak committability must not count against the design.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: pg_rewind reads pg_control and rewrites data files of an unclean target without recovery having updated the control file first.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: pg_rewind now finds the end of target WAL and the pre-divergence checkpoint by its own scan.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-3: Stale postmaster.pid removal by PID check alone can expose a live cluster

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: pg_rewind takes over work that server crash recovery did, and the patch removes the --no-ensure-shutdown option.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: No field evidence that crash recovery dominates real rewind time

questions: For a target that crashed after promotion but before its first checkpoint, which timeline and checkpoint does pg_rewind use, and how does it derive them?
Which control-file fields does pg_rewind now trust as read, and which does it derive from the WAL scan?
Which end-of-recovery actions of the server does the scan not perform, and what test fails if the scan and crash recovery reach different end points?
What interlock beyond a PID existence check stops pg_rewind from removing postmaster.pid when the postmaster is dead but orphaned backends still run?
Why can --no-ensure-shutdown not stay as an accepted no-op, with the pg_rewind documentation updated to match?

committability.owner_note: The owner needs to know crash recovery, xlogreader and timeline handling as well as pg_rewind. Nobody has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of every rewind of an unclean target, with no time limit. A wrong timeline or end point shows up later as a standby that fails to start or holds diverged blocks.
committability.author_follow_up: The author moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October. The thread shows no rebased version after the CFbot notice in September.

priority.reason: Rewinding a crashed old primary is a common use of pg_rewind, and the benchmark shows 25% to 37% shorter runs. The patch is about 27 KiB in pg_rewind only, but review needs recovery knowledge, and the control-file and interlock questions come before code review.

provisional_note: The code was not read. The patch may already derive the target timeline from WAL or check shared memory before it removes postmaster.pid; the prose does not say either.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_rewind does not rewind diverging timelines
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stores a UUID for each timeline in the timeline history file, so pg_rewind can tell apart two servers that were promoted to the same TLI on their own. When the TLIs match but the UUIDs differ, pg_rewind goes back to the last timeline where both the TLI and the UUID match and rewinds from there.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The reviewers asked only for small fixes, and the author made them. The last message reports that the new 005_same_timeline test fails on Windows CI because the restore_command path is mangled, and no reply follows before the entry was withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Data-only mode for pg_rewind
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a --data-only flag to pg_rewind so it rewinds only the minimal set of files needed for the cluster to work, leaving other files in the data directory alone. Default behavior does not change.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Thomas Munro returned the entry with feedback because the author did not respond to his request to rebase the bitrotted patch. Earlier, Michael Paquier objected that rewinding only a fixed set of files can break pg_rewind when a newly added data directory folder holds non-replaceable data needed at the start of recovery. Stephen Frost supported the idea and suggested one canonical list of needed files.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I set this to "Returned with feedback" due to lack of response.

precedents_retrieved.title: Restrict pg_rewind to specified/needed directories
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, David Steele, Stephen Frost
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_rewind synchronize only a fixed list of directories (base, global, pg_wal, pg_xact and other WAL-related directories), so it no longer copies logs, replication slots or configuration files from the source. The list of files is fetched with one query per listed directory.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to an include list: a directory missing from it, such as one added by a new feature or an extension, can make a rewind silently corrupt. They asked pg_rewind to reuse the exclude list that base backups already use, by moving it to common code, and to add an option for more exclusions. The patch stayed in Waiting on Author, and Michael Paquier returned it with feedback and said he would work on the exclude-list approach himself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Forgetting something in the
exclusion list just makes the process less efficient while forgetting
something in the inclusion list may mean breakage.

precedents_retrieved.title: Make pg_rewind not copy useless WALs
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change pg_rewind so it skips WAL segments that come before the divergence point, which the target already has. It also skips segments after the source's current WAL insert location, such as recycled future segments.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message, from Alexander Korotkov, says the code looks good but the patch lacks documentation updates, including the paragraph that says which files pg_rewind copies. No later reply from the author is shown before the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add tablespace tap test to pg_rewind
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a TAP test for pg_rewind that checks tablespaces created before and after standby promotion, modeled on 002_databases.pl. It extends RewindTest.pm, PostgresNode.pm and RecursiveCopy.pm so a standby can be built with tablespace mapping and symlinks can be copied.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The test setup made the primary, the backup and the standbys share the same tablespace paths, so multiple standbys from one backup would use one tablespace directory and the source and target servers would overwrite each other. A correct test needs a tablespace mapping option for the file-level backup routines in RecursiveCopy.pm and PostgresNode::init_from_backup, and an option in pg_rewind similar to pg_basebackup's --tablespace-mapping. Michael Paquier judged this a large amount of work that may be hard to justify.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And on top of that there is of course the argument of pg_rewind which
would need an option similar to pg_basebackup's --tablespace-mapping
so as a target instance does not finish by using the same tablespace
path as the source where there is a tablespace of difference during
the operation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid Copying WAL Segments Before Divergence to Speed Up pg_rewind
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_rewind skip copying WAL segments that come before the segment holding the last common checkpoint, since source and target share them. The author reported that WAL files are over 95% of the data pg_rewind copies in their setups.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not answer Michael Paquier's review of 2022-10-06, so the entry was marked returned with feedback. That review asked for tests that use command_checks_all() instead of reading log files, and an assertion that the WAL segment exists on both sides. It also asked about segments with older timelines and for WAL segments to be tracked in file_entry_t. Alexander Korotkov saw no design objections in the thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This review has been done a few weeks ago, and there has been no
update since, so I am marking this entry as returned with feedback in
the CF app.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_rewind with cascade standby doesn't work well
precedents_retrieved.summary: When a cascading standby replays the end-of-recovery record of its upstream's promotion, the patch has it request an immediate restartpoint. The control file then shows the new timeline, so pg_rewind can use the standby as source right away instead of reporting "same timeline". An earlier version set minRecoveryPoint and minRecoveryPointTLI in xlog_redo, but that broke crash recovery.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last review came in July 2024 and no author reply is visible before the entry was returned. That review found that v3 no longer applied to master. It asked whether making WAL replay wait for the restartpoint hurts performance, and noted the behaviour change was not documented. It also proposed a less invasive fix, where pg_rewind detects the case and runs a checkpoint on the standby.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Regarding the approach to force a checkpoint on every restartpoint record, I wonder if it has any performance implications, since now the WAL replay will wait for the restartpoint to finish as opposed to it happening in the background.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes how pg_rewind finds the end of WAL on the target, so that shutdown checkpoint and WAL switch records after the divergence point are skipped. A clean failover where the old primary wrote only a shutdown checkpoint would then report that no rewind is needed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said the premise is wrong: the shutdown checkpoint updates the control file, which matters when deciding whether servers are in sync, and the server itself refuses to follow the new timeline. A clean shutdown also writes a RUNNING_XACTS record, which the patch did not skip. A later version from another poster did not address these points, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I do not think we can do
that, because (1) those WAL records might do important things like
update the control file and (2) the server will not be OK with
ignoring those WAL records even if pg_rewind decides that they are not
important.

roaster_notes.note: P4, P6 and P9 also aimed to speed up pg_rewind, but they ended without review answers and recorded no design reason that applies here. P7 shares only the area.
Other contract points, such as control-file state after rewind, are left to the safety angle.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect: pg_rewind runs as the data directory owner, and the patch adds no role, function, view or setting. Removing a postmaster.pid whose PID is not visible, for example from another container or host on shared storage, is a data-safety risk and belongs to the safety angle.

No existing feature, option or extension gives the same result. Today the only path for an unclean target is the single-user crash recovery that pg_rewind runs itself, and the patch speeds up that path instead of adding a second one. End-of-WAL detection reuses the WAL scan pg_rewind already does with the shared xlogreader, so a duplicated mechanism is not apparent from the prose; safety and option removal belong to other angles.
Rewinding a crashed old primary is a common pg_rewind use, so the problem is real. Demand for this speedup has not been shown.
